persons.name: F.C. Berger
persons.note: PROJECTED RESIDENT. Documented in Chicago post-office evidence but not independently corroborated strongly enough for attested circa-1835 residence. KNOWN ONLY FROM THE POST OFFICE, IN ONE RETURN. The papers print 'Berger, F.C,' in a single return of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office — the Democrat of 20 May 1835, column 13 — dated 1835-05-20. Nothing else in the corpus names this person: no trade, no street, no household, no arrival, so every other claim here is written unattested in its own block. WHAT THAT IS WORTH: a correspondent believed a person of this name reachable at Chicago on that date, and nothing further — not that they lived here, kept a trade here, or were here on 1 July 1835. It is the weakest evidence this project accepts for a resident, and a source placing them elsewhere retires the record. THE ARGUMENT EVERY RECORD OF THIS KIND SHARES is written once instead of once per file: the ruling of 2026-08-30 and what it cost the town (docs/LIBERTIES.md L214), the refusals and the transcription standard behind the reading (tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py). persons.name: G. W. Keeney
persons.note: A DOCUMENTED PERSON, AND NOTHING ELSE IS CLAIMED. The papers name 'G. W. KEENEY' and give the trade; they do not say where this household lived, who else was in it, or when it came. So the record around this person carries nothing but the person: no dwelling, no division, no family, each written as unattested in its own block rather than filled in from the shape of the rest of the town. Cited at the Democrat of 7 May 1834, column 3. The corpus associates the name with Chicago; that is where the paper does business with this person and not a statement about where they slept, and the storefront tickets are the ones that may stand a shop there. THE TOWN NEVER INVENTED A ROOF FOR THIS TRADE. The occupation census raised reconstructed households for the trades a town of 3,265 people needed and could not document; `founder` was not one of them, which is why this person could only ever be ADDED and never seated on an existing record — data/research/newspapers/register_1835.json calls it `new_resident` for exactly that reason. No figure is drawn (docs/LIBERTIES.md L1). READ THROUGH A TRANSCRIPTION, not a scan: the owner's ruling of 2026-08-28 grades a transcription-mediated reading as documented, and the source record for the run states that standard and its limits. A scan read that confirms or corrects the name upgrades this entry.

persons.name: James H Mulford
persons.note: THE 1835 POLL LIST AND A SECOND INDEPENDENT SOURCE. Read from newspaper_1833_1835, poll_1834, poll_1835, tax_1833. THE GRADE IS THE OWNER'S RATIFIED LADDER OF 2026-09-03 (G1a), applied to every identity at once by tools/consolidate_resident_evidence.py and spent onto this card by tools/mint_civic_residents.py; the evidence blocks below carry the reading AS READ, its locator and the record it came from, so the page can be gone back to. WHAT IS RECONSTRUCTED: everything except the person and the sources — no dwelling, no trade, no origin, no family, no party. A BOUND FROM THE RECORD, NOT AN ARRIVAL. tax_1833 stands against this person's name by 31 December 1833 and nothing says when they came. THE 1833 TAX LIST IS A PROPERTY ROLL, NOT A RESIDENCE CHECK (T-1117): it names the owner of ground inside the town, resident or not, and its own entry 110 is a man three years dead. It bounds the town's RECORD of this name and not the day this person reached Chicago. The bound is at or before the scene date, so the town's own paper carries this name by 1 July 1835; whether the man it names was standing in the town is a claim this record cannot make, and present_on_scene_date says `uncertain` for that reason. No figure is drawn (L1). THE TOWN'S OWN ROLLS, 1833-1835 — CORROBORATION, NOT A GRADE. The early Chicago voter and tax lists held by the Illinois Regional Archives Depository name this person 3 times: Tax list of the Town of Chicago, 1833 — “Mulford, James H.” (tax_1833_077, line 129); Election returns — poll list of 1834, filed 11 August 1834 — “Mulford, J. H.” (poll_1834_077, line 246); Poll list of 1835 — “Mulford, J. H.” (poll_1835_050, line 337). These are the town's own contemporary paper rather than a recollection of it, and each appearance says that a man of that name stood on that roll in that year — no more. The reading is twice mediated (Schulz's transcription, then Genealogy Trails' republication) and this project has not seen the IRAD originals. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the 1835 poll with a second independent source is attested, the 1835 poll alone or a 1833/1834 list with another source is inferred, and a single appearance with nothing else is a projected resident. This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE — T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: one resident of the surname 'Mulford' agrees with the entry's forenames; 2 bearer(s) of the surname were considered. (data/research/civic/voter_crosswalk.json). THE FEDERAL LAND TRACT SALES — A PURCHASE, AND NEVER A RESIDENCE. The Illinois State Archives' Public Domain Land Tract Sales register enters this person 6 times, as “MULFORD JAMES H”, “MULFORD J H”, 1833-10-25 to 1836-06-28: 4 lots in the platted town — lot 2 of block 3 in the town the register codes CHI (L2BL3CHI, as printed); lot 3 of block 3 in the town the register codes CHI (L3BL3CHI, as printed); lot 3 of block 6 in the town the register codes CHI (L3BL6CHI, as printed); lot 9 of block 46 in the town the register codes CHIOT (L9BL46CHIOT, as printed) and 2 parcels of the school section — lot 8 of block 119 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E); lot 8 of block 96 of the school section (sec 16 T39N R14E), 0.00 acres stated in all, for $8515.00 (ls0285, ls0286, ls1388, ls1389, ls1390, ls1387). THE REGISTER'S OWN RESIDENCE COLUMN READS UNKNOWN on these rows: a county, a state or nothing, and never a town, which is why a purchase here places nobody. THE SCHOOL-SECTION ROWS ARE GROUND INSIDE THE TOWN, NOT FARMLAND: section 16 of T39N R14E was platted and sold off by lot and by block at the sale of 1833, which is why the register states 0000.00 acres against most of them. Ground inside the town is nearer to this reconstruction than a quarter-section is, and it is still a purchase: the register names a purchaser and never an occupant, and nothing here puts this person on that ground. THE TOWN LOTS ARE THE PLAT ITSELF, AND THEY ARE NOT ACRES: Cook County's register describes them by lot and block in a platted town and gives them no section, no township and no acreage at all, so they add nothing to the acre figure above and $8240.00 to the money. This project does not expand the register's town codes, so which addition a lot stands in is carried as the code and not as a name. It is still a purchase and it still places nobody. A purchase and nothing more. It dates and places a transaction; it proposes no residence, and under the ratified ladder it corroborates rather than mints. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: MULFORD JAMES H matches James H Mulford: the forename names James H Mulford of the 2 people of this surname, and the forename agrees in full. (data/research/land_sales/resident_crosswalk.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a land entry is a second source about a TRANSACTION rather than about who was living at Chicago on 1 July 1835 — a man may buy a quarter-section he never sees. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict.

persons.name: John M. Nelson
persons.note: PROJECTED RESIDENT. Documented in Chicago post-office evidence but not independently corroborated strongly enough for attested circa-1835 residence. KNOWN ONLY FROM THE POST OFFICE, IN ONE RETURN. The papers print 'Nelson, John M, &' in a single return of letters uncalled-for at the Chicago post office — the Democrat of 20 May 1835, column 13 — dated 1835-05-20. Nothing else in the corpus names this person: no trade, no street, no household, no arrival, so every other claim here is written unattested in its own block. WHAT THAT IS WORTH: a correspondent believed a person of this name reachable at Chicago on that date, and nothing further — not that they lived here, kept a trade here, or were here on 1 July 1835. It is the weakest evidence this project accepts for a resident, and a source placing them elsewhere retires the record. THE ARGUMENT EVERY RECORD OF THIS KIND SHARES is written once instead of once per file: the ruling of 2026-08-30 and what it cost the town (docs/LIBERTIES.md L214), the refusals and the transcription standard behind the reading (tools/mint_letter_list_residents.py). No figure is drawn (L1). FERGUS 1839'S LATER LISTS — 1837 AND 1839 EVIDENCE, NEVER AN 1835 FACT. Fergus' Chicago Directory for 1839 names this person 1 time in its two later lists: the city register of 1839 — “John A. Nelson” as sheriff of cook county, 1864 (f1839_r0104, printed page 39). What a match may carry, and it depends on WHICH TABLE it landed in. A match on printed page 38, or on any row of the mayors' table, is 1839-or-later evidence: it says the man held that office in that year and was therefore in Chicago in that year, it is written with the row's own describes_date and never as an 1835 fact, and the person's grade does not move on it alone — a later appearance is corroboration of CONTINUED RESIDENCE, not of July 1835. A match on the sheriffs' rows of 1831, 1832, 1834 or 1836 is different in kind: the office is contemporary with the town, the 1834 row's term covers the scene date outright, and such a match carries reaches_scene. Even there the SOURCE is a retrospect — a table running to 1874, set in 1876 out of Old Settlers' recollections per the compiler's warning on printed page 3 — so it may be cited as a contemporary office and may not be graded `documented` without a second, nearer record. The ward on printed page 38 is a ward of the CITY of 1839 and places no house in the town of 1835. Identity by the crosswalk's own rule: Surname 'Nelson' folds to the same string as the register entry's, and the given name of both begins J. (data/research/directories/fergus_1839_election_crosswalk_1835.json and fergus_1839_register_crosswalk_1835.json). This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE. Under the ratified ladder (T-0513) a second independent source is what lifts a projected resident, and a poll twenty-two months after the scene date — or a register four years after it — is a second source about CONTINUED RESIDENCE rather than about July 1835. T-0515 applies the ladder against every source at once; this pass hands it the evidence and not the verdict. THE SECOND PRESBYTERIAN ROLL — A NAME ON A CHURCH LIST THAT OPENS IN 1842, AND NEVER AN 1835 FACT. The 1892 printed membership roll of the Second Presbyterian Church of Chicago, read line by line into this repository, carries 1 line whose surname and given initial agree with this person's — “Nelson, Miss Jane | Profession. | September 30, 1870. | Dismissed.” (second_presb_0765, printed page 196), admitted 1870-09-30 by profession. Under the rule that decided it: Surname 'Nelson' folds to the same string as the roll line's, and the given name of both begins J. WHAT THE MATCH MINTS OR REGRADES: “NOTHING. A line on a roll that opens in June 1842 cannot place a person in the town of July 1835, and this file makes no proposal that it does. What a match IS: the same surname and initial, in Chicago, within seven years — a lead for a later pass that is allowed to write people.” This pass WRITES THE EVIDENCE AND MOVES NO GRADE: under the ratified ladder (T-0513) the roll is handed to the card as a thing a reader may weigh, and the verdict stays with T-0515, which applies the ladder against every source at once.

residents.research_note: RECONSTRUCTED HOUSEHOLD — no trade recorded, in the south division, where it is counted after the re-family recorded above; it was drawn in the south division. NOBODY HERE IS NAMED BY ANY SOURCE. The 1840 Chicago schedule counts children under ten at 27% of the town and women of twenty to twenty-nine as its second-largest band; the 1835 layer the sources can name holds 15 women, because the rolls that name this town — a letter list, a voters' roll, a subscription — print men. That gap is the shape of the evidence and not a reading of the town, so the order book counts it bucket by bucket and this household is drawn against those counts. Every value on it carries the model row and the seed that redraws it, and a source naming a woman who kept her own house in this division retires the whole record. No figure is drawn (docs/LIBERTIES.md L1). This household is one of the surplus the re-cut HOLDS rather than retires: the owner's ruling of 2026-09-24 re-families it into a cell the book still orders instead of un-writing it, and `refamilied` above is the whole of what that changed.

what_it_supplies: A 665-roof production target with independently reconcilable group, district, level, and construction totals.
Thirty-five architectural family definitions with dimensional and massing bands.
District character, spacing, variation, finish, and chronology constraints for a July 1835 reconstruction.
A required distinction between named documentary landmarks and anonymous inferred infill.
what_it_does_not_supply: A surviving July 1835 building census or parcel-by-parcel roof register.
Exact locations, dimensions, appearance, occupants, or construction dates for anonymous roofs.
Authority to replace stronger building-specific evidence already represented in the dataset.

research_note: RECONSTRUCTED / GENERATED, NOT AN ATTESTED NAMED BUILDING. The block, its scheduled roof count and its family mix follow the 665-roof programme; exact presence, lot, position, footprint, finish and instance-level form are interpretive. H-family house massing currently resolves through the frame dwelling archetype; no larger house generator is implemented. THE CENTRE HALL IS THE ENTRY'S, NOT THIS PARCEL'S (T-1686). H1 is the only family of the thirty-five whose crosswalk entry names a centre hall and states a bare bay count — its required variant is "center_hall_one_and_half" and its variants line reads "5 bays; center hall; kitchen ell; small porch" — so the plan and the bay count below are read off that entry and not dealt by this parcel. The kitchen ell and the small porch the same line offers are NOT raised with them: both are selectable variants beside the required one, and an ell is a footprint fact this record's rectangle does not carry.
